## Motivation

[Characterization and Identification of Productivity-Associated Rhizobacteria in Wheat, Anderson and Habiger, *Applied and Environmental Microbiology* (2012)](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aem.07466-11)

From the Abstract: "The rhizosphere is populated by a numerous and diverse array of rhizobacteria, and many impact productivity in largely unknown ways... **Operational taxonomic units (OTUs) that were significantly associated with biomass productivity were _identified using an exact test adjusted for the false-discovery rate_**..."

## Question: Standardize?

- **PCA Objective**: Retain as much variation as possible with fewer new variables Z1, Z2,...


- Typically PCA is ran after scaling **variables** to have standard deviation 1.  This way unit of measure doesn't matter <br>

- Here we ran PCA on logged **samples**  <br>

- Are data already on the "same scale" across samples? <br>

  - If yes, scaling won't affect PCA analysis <br>

# Part 2: FDR-adjusted discoveries

## Generic Procedure for FDR control

The False Discovery Rate (FDR) is
$$FDR = E\left[\frac{\# \text{ False Discoveries}}{\#\text{ Discoveries} }\right]$$

1. Specify statistical model and null hypotheses $H_1, H_2,..., H_M$

2. Compute p-values $p_1,p_2,..,p_M$ or posterior null probabilities $q_1,q_2,...,q_M$ 

3. Use statistics above to estimate FDR or "adjust" for FDR

  - [B-H estimate](https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x): $\widehat{FDR}(p_{(k)}) = \frac{M p_{(k)}}{k}$ <br> 
  
  - [Empirical Bayes estimate](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/016214507000000545): $\widehat{FDR}(q_{(k)}) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k q_{(i)}$ 

## Example: BH procedure

```{r, echo = TRUE}
pvalues=rep(NULL, 778)
lfc=rep(NULL, 778)
bacteria = as.matrix(bacteria)
for(i in 1:778){
  #1. Specify model
  model=summary(glm(bacteria[i,]~biomass, family="poisson"))
  #2. Compute p-values (and LFC while we're at it)
  pvalues[i]=model$coefficient[2,4]
  lfc[i]=model$coefficient[2,1]
}
```

- Warnings!  Really!  Models don't get much simpler than this! 

- See STAT 5093 learn what happened.     
  

## Example: BH continued.

```{r, echo = TRUE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3.5}
# 3. Estimate FDR and return TRUE if < .05
discoveries = p.adjust(pvalues, method = "BH")<.05
sum(discoveries)
plot(pvalues, p.adjust(pvalues, method="BH"), ylab="FDR", xlim = c(0,.05),ylim=c(0,.5), col= as.numeric(discoveries)+1)
abline(h = 0.05,v=.05, lwd =c(5,1), col = c(2,1))
legend("topleft", inset=.05, col=2, pch=1, legend = "Discovery")
```

## Q: Why not p < .05? 

- Q: How many discoveries would be made?
```{r, echo = TRUE}
NumDiscoveries = sum(pvalues<.05)
NumDiscoveries
```

- Q: How many false discoveries would be anticipated?
```{r, echo = TRUE}
NumFalseDiscoveries = 778*.05
NumFalseDiscoveries
```

- Q: What is the FDR of this procedure? Is it acceptable?
```{r, echo = TRUE}
38.9/135
```



## Example: Empirical Bayes Procedure

```{r, echo = TRUE}
#1. Priors pi, beta estimated in Habiger, Watts, Anderson (2017)
pi = c(.69,.16,.15)
beta=c(0,-1.13,.78)

#2 Compute posterior: 
p.0=exp(beta[1]*biomass)/sum(exp(beta[1]*biomass))
p.l=exp(beta[2]*biomass)/sum(exp(beta[2]*biomass))
p.u=exp(beta[3]*biomass)/sum(exp(beta[3]*biomass))
q<-function(y){ pi[1]*dmultinom(y,prob=p.0)/
 (pi[1]*dmultinom(y,prob=p.0) + pi[2]*dmultinom(y,prob=p.l)+pi[3]*dmultinom(y, prob=p.u))}
qs=rep(NULL, 778)
for(i in 1:778){qs[i]=q(bacteria[i,])}
```

- Notable differences in steps 1 and 2

    - Specified pi and beta values
    
    - Had to use Bayes theorem to compute $q$ manually -  not using glm()

## Example: Emp. Bayes Procedure cont.

```{r, echo=TRUE,fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3}
#3 EBdiscoveries are ones with FDR<.05
s.q=sort(qs)
FDR=cumsum(s.q)/1:778
k=sum(FDR<=.05)
EBdiscoveries=qs<=s.q[k]
sum(EBdiscoveries)

plot(s.q, FDR, xlab="Post. Null", ylab = "FDR", xlim = c(0,.3), ylim = c(0, .1), col=I(FDR<.05)+1)
abline(h = 0.05, lwd =5, col = 2)
legend("topleft", inset=.05, col=2, pch=1, legend = "Discovery")
```

## Before FDR adjustment
```{r, fig.width=8, echo=TRUE}
biplot(princomp(l.bacteria[,]),scale=0)
```

## After BH FDR Adjustment
```{r, fig.width=8, echo=TRUE}
biplot(princomp(l.bacteria[discoveries,]),xlim = c(-3,8),ylim = c(-4, 4),scale=0)
```

## After EB FDR Adjustment
```{r, fig.width=8, echo=TRUE}
biplot(princomp(l.bacteria[EBdiscoveries,]),xlim = c(-3,8),ylim = c(-4, 4), scale=0)
```

## BH vs. Emp. Bayes FDR adjustment 

```{r, echo= TRUE}
plot(lfc,p.adjust(pvalues, method="BH"), xlim = c(-3,3), xlab = "log fold change", ylab=expression(hat(FDR)))
abline(h=0.05, lwd =3) 
#index=sort(qs, index=TRUE)[[2]]
#points(lfc[index], FDR,pch=2, col=2)
legend("topright",legend=c("BH","Emp Bayes"), pch = c(1,2), col = c(1,2))
```

## BH vs. Emp. Bayes FDR adjustment 
```{r, echo= TRUE}
plot(lfc,p.adjust(pvalues, method="BH"), xlim = c(-3,3), xlab = "log fold change", ylab=expression(hat(FDR)))
abline(h=0.05, lwd =3) 
index=sort(qs, index=TRUE)[[2]]
points(lfc[index], FDR,pch=2, col=2)
legend("topright",legend=c("BH","Emp Bayes"), pch = c(1,2), col = c(1,2))
```

# Part 3: FDR Methods Research

## P-value FDR Methods Questions

- Properties: BH procedure controls the FDR **If P-values are valid** and positively correlated.  

- FDR methods research asks questions in each step of the analysis. 

- Step 1. We specified Poisson model and null hypothesis $H_0: LFC_i = 0$ (the log fold change in abundance per biomass gram for bacteria $i$) 

  - Over-dispersion: Try adding "family = quasipoisson" to glm(), or using nb.glm(), chisq.test(), lm() on logged data? Do you get the same results? Why? 
  
  - Zero inflation: What about all of the zeros in the data and "zero inflation"
    
  - Normalization: Try glm(bacteria[i,]~biomass + s,..) where $s$ is column total (or proportion).  Based on PCA, what do you think?
  
  - What is overfitting and why does it matter above?
    
  - Why $H_0:LFC_i = 0$ and why not $H_0:LFC_i\approx 0$?
    
## P-value FDR Methods Questions

- Step 2. Compute $Z_i = \widehat{LFC}_i/SE_i$ and $P_i=\Pr_0(|Z_i|\geq |z_i|)$

  - P-values are valid only if we use the **correct distribution** on the previous slide. Which distribution is correct in the previous slide?

  - Why would standard errors (and hence p-values) tend to be very small for abundant bacteria? 
  
  - Who cares?  What does this have to do with the Null Hypothesis of Interest $H_0: LFC_i\approx 0$ vs usual $H_0:LFC_i = 0$. 

## Technically H0 is false

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=5,fig.cap='Statistics Show Fred is Associated with Productivity'}
knitr::include_graphics("cartoon.jpg")
```




## P-value FDR Methods Questions

- Properties: BH procedure controls the FDR ''**If P-values are valid**`` and positively correlated.  

- FDR methods research asks questions in each step of the analysis. 

- Step 3. Compute $FDR(p) = \frac{M p}{(\# p_i\leq p)}$

    - The numerator estimates # False Discoveries as M $p$.  Is that conservative? 
  
    - Can we use $SE_i$ in weighted p-value procedures? 
  
## Empirical Bayes FDR Questions
- Properties: Empirical Bayes procedures **should** (asymptotically) control the  and [make more discoveries than p-value methods counterparts](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/016214507000000545)

- Step 1. Assumed multinomial distribution and tested $H_0:LFC_i=0$ with

    - $LFC_i$ = 0 with probability 0.69
    - $LFC_i$ = -1.13 with probability 0.16, or  
    - $LFC_i$ = .78 with probability 0.15

- Prior estimation: Why MLE's in Habiger, Watts, Anderson? Other estimators?
  
- Over-dispersion: What other priors could we consider? Gamma prior? 
    
- Normalization: Try adding column totals or proportions to ``beta[k] biomass''      
- Is $H_0:LFC_i = 0$ or $H_i:LFC_i\approx 0$ tested?


## Empirical Bayes FDR Questions

- Step 2. Compute **posterior null probability** $q_i = \Pr(LFC_i=0|\text{Bacteria}_i)$

    - Posterior Nulls are "valid" **IF** a) model is flexible enough b) priors estimated parameters well.   
      
      - Is it flexible enough? Are they estimated well?
      
      - Bias Variance tradeoff, over/under fitting, etc.
      
      - "if and only if" or just "if"? 

    - Does posterior null probability change if $H_0:LFC_i\approx 0$ vs $H_0:LFC_i = 0$ for more flexible models?    
    

  

## Empirical Bayes FDR Questions

- Step 3. Estimate $FDR(q_{(r)}) = \bar{q}$ 

  - We could prove that **ANY DISCOVERY RULE** with $\bar{q}\leq \alpha$ controls FDR!  

    - Before we discovered the smallest posterior nulls b/c we wanted to maximize number of discoveries.
    
    - Quantity vs quality?
    
    - How to measure "quality" 
  
## Empirical Bayes vs Classical FDR

- Why is the [Benjamini and Hochber (1995) procedure](https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x) one of the most [highly cited statistics papers of all time](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZGU4SlE9Pu8)? 

    - Try changing ``sum(p.adjust(pvalues, method = "BH")<.05)`` to 
  ``sum(pvalues <.05/length(pvalues))`` - That used to be our only option.    

    - We can get usually get a p-value for quite complex models  
  
    - Don't have to estimate a prior 

- When to use an Empirical Bayes methods?

    - You know how to specify and estimate prior / model parameters well 

    - To develop / study classical procedures

## More Questions for ??? 

- Rhizosphere-Mediated Effects on Winter Wheat Yield in Oklahoma and the Development of Diagnostic Probes targeting beneficial microorganisms, Ramos-Lopez, Espindola, et. al. (2026+)  

- Model: Log Abundance $\sim$ LFC $\times f(\text{Phenotype}_1,..., \text{Phenotype}_5)$
    
    - $f()$ returns Low or High productivity
    
    - 12 trt groups (Soil x Variety x Feek Stage) +  3 sampling depths

- [HD Replicability Analysis](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/statistical-science/volume-38/issue-4/Replicability-Across-Multiple-Studies/10.1214/23-STS892.pdf) could be used to identify bacteria differentially expressed in $2$ + groups, $3$ + groups, ? 
  
  
- [HD Mediation Analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7263455/) could be used to identify which bacteria are mediating relationships between factors and yield?  

- In both emerging fields, we have all modeling challenges as before + the choice  estimate of $f$ to consider. 

## Huizi Wang (PhD 2026)

- Efficient Classification Methods for Sparse High-Dimensional Count Data with Model Selection as Motivated by Microbe Finder

$$\text{logit}(\Pr(\text{Pathogen})) = \beta_1 EP_1 + \beta_2 EP_2 + ... +\beta_{1000} EP_{1000}$$

- Competing Methods: 
  - Logistic Regression with LASSO penalty 
  - Quadratic Discriminant Analysis on total = EP1 +...+EP1000 for overfitting

- Huizi's Method and Contributions
  - Add dummy variables to above equation to allow for zero inflation 
  - Simple (closed form) estimates under zero inflated over disp model
  - "soft thresholding" (like LASSO) to shrink estimates and select Eprobe
  - Better prediction power (AUROC) than either method! Surprising!  

## Chase Cao (PhD 2024)
The Backstory

1. Ioannidis: [Why Most Published Research Findings are False](
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124) - sciencewide FDR!

2. ASA (ish) [statement on p-values](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108) blames $p$-value misuses for crisis.

3. Benjamini clarifies that its [Selective inference: The Silent Killer of Replicability](https://hdsr.mitpress.mit.edu/pub/l39rpgyc/release/3)

Working **Selective Inference** Model for Science: 

  1. All "data" in some population  
  2. **Selection mechanism** say $\delta = [P<.05]$ -> observable data 
  3. Inference on health of scientific ecosystem with selected data

Question: Is $\delta$ really that simple? What if we're wrong? 

  - Chase et al. ``Sensitivity Analysis for FDR Estimation Under Misspecified Selection Model''
